title: Paul's Powers and Principalities
bigQuestion: Who are the rulers, authorities and powers in Paul's letters, and why have readers answered so differently?

story.title: A List on the Board
story.kicker: A high school teacher writes Paul's list of powers on the board and asks one simple question that fills the whole hour.
paragraphs: It is a Tuesday afternoon in a high school classroom. Ms. Ortiz picks up a marker and writes a list on the whiteboard: thrones, dominions, principalities, powers. Under it she writes one line from the King James Version: 'For by him were all things created, that are in heaven, and that are in earth, visible and invisible.' Then she writes the reference: Colossians 1:16.

She turns around. 'Paul uses these words again and again,' she says. 'Rulers. Authorities. Powers. So here is today's question. Who are they?' A student in the front row says they must be kings and governors. Another says the verse says invisible, so they must be angels. A third wonders if Paul means something like systems, the way people talk about 'the powers that be'.

Ms. Ortiz writes all three answers on the board. 'Good,' she says. 'Scholars have given every one of those answers. Some have given all three at once.' She adds a fourth line: Deuteronomy 32:8. 'Michael Heiser, a scholar of the Hebrew Bible, argued that this verse is the key. He thought Paul's powers are the gods of the nations that the Hebrew Bible talks about.'

The class spends the rest of the hour reading. They look at Ephesians, Colossians, Romans, 1 Corinthians and Galatians. They compare the Greek words behind the English. By the end, no one agrees on everything. But everyone can explain why readers disagree. That is where this chapter will take you, too.
story.think: Why might Paul use words like 'thrones' and 'rulers', which sound political, for beings he also calls invisible?

lessons.title: A List of Rulers
lessons.mainIdea: Paul often lists rulers, authorities, powers, dominions and thrones, words that describe beings by the territory or rank they hold.
reading: Ephesians 1:20–21 says God raised Christ and seated him at his right hand in the heavenly places. He is far above all rule, authority, power and dominion, and every name that is named. Colossians 1:16 says all things were created through him, in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones, dominions, rulers or authorities. Paul returns to the same set of words again and again.

Behind the English stand Greek words. *Archai* means rulers or beginnings; the King James Version says 'principalities'. *Exousiai* means authorities, often translated 'powers'. *Dynameis* means powers or mighty ones. *Kyriotētes* means dominions or lordships, and *thronoi* means thrones. Every one of these words was also used for human government. They describe someone by the rank or territory they control.

Heiser noticed this. In The Unseen Realm (2015) and Demons (2020), he argued that Paul used these ruling words for spiritual beings on purpose. They describe beings who hold territory, like governors over lands. Some Jewish writings from Paul's time used similar words for heavenly beings. For Heiser, this was not random. It was the language of the gods of the nations, the rebel members of what he called the *divine council*.

words.d: Greek for rulers or beginnings; translated 'principalities' in the King James Version
Greek for authorities; often translated 'powers'
the territory or rule that someone controls; in Greek, kyriotēs
Heiser's term for God's heavenly assembly of elohim, or spiritual beings, described in texts like Psalm 82

look.title: How Many Powers in Each List?
look.cite: Counted in the King James Version (1611): e.g. Colossians 1:16 names thrones, dominions, principalities and powers
look.prompt: Paul and 1 Peter both list powers. Look up two of these verses. Which words repeat across the lists? What does the repetition suggest?

check.q: What does the Greek word archai mean?
check.why: Archai means rulers or beginnings; the King James Version translates it 'principalities'.

check.q: Which verse says all things were created through Christ, including thrones and dominions?
check.why: Colossians 1:16 names thrones, dominions, rulers and authorities as created things.

check.q: According to Heiser, why did Paul use ruling words for spiritual beings?
choices: Paul did not know any other words
They were words from Hesiod's poems
They were names of Roman emperors
They describe beings who hold territory, like the gods of the nations
check.why: Heiser argued these words describe spiritual beings who rule territory, the rebel members of the divine council.

lessons.title: In the Heavenly Places
lessons.mainIdea: Ephesians 6:12 says the struggle is not against flesh and blood but against rulers and authorities in the heavenly places.
reading: Ephesians 6:12 is Paul's most famous list of powers. It says the struggle is not against flesh and blood. It is against rulers, against authorities, against the world-rulers of this darkness and against spiritual forces of evil in the *heavenly places*. The King James Version says 'high places'. The Greek phrase is the same one Ephesians uses for where Christ is seated (1:20).

One word here is rare. *Kosmokratores* means world-rulers. It appears only here in the New Testament. In Greek writings of the time it could describe powerful gods thought to rule the world. So Ephesians is describing beings, not only human leaders. The very next verses talk about truth, righteousness, peace, faith and the word of God, pictured as armor. The passage calls on readers to stand firm.

Heiser read this verse as a summary of his whole view of Paul. The powers are real spiritual rulers in the heavenly realm, he argued, and they oppose God's people. Other readers point out that the letter also has plenty to say about human life: families, work and the way people treat each other. Many see the passage as describing both unseen powers and their effects on human life. It is a call to stand firm, not a set of steps or rituals.

words.d: the phrase in Ephesians for the unseen realm; the King James Version says 'high places' in 6:12
Greek for world-rulers, found in the New Testament only in Ephesians 6:12
a Hebrew and Greek expression for human beings

look.title: Ephesians 6:12
look.text: For we wrestle not against flesh and blood, but against principalities, against powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual wickedness in high places.
look.prompt: The verse first says who the struggle is not against. Why do you think the writer starts with that? Which phrase translates kosmokratores?

check.q: According to Ephesians 6:12, the struggle is NOT against what?
check.why: The verse says the struggle is not against flesh and blood, meaning human beings.

check.q: What does kosmokratores mean?
check.why: Kosmokratores means world-rulers; it appears only in Ephesians 6:12 in the New Testament.

check.q: Where else does Ephesians use the phrase 'heavenly places'?
choices: For where Christ is seated in 1:20
check.why: Ephesians 1:20 says Christ is seated at God's right hand in the heavenly places.

lessons.title: Nothing Can Separate
lessons.mainIdea: Romans 8:38–39 names angels, rulers and powers among the things that cannot separate believers from God's love, as Paul tells it.
reading: Romans 8 ends with one of Paul's best-known passages. He says he is convinced that nothing can separate believers from the love of God in Christ Jesus. Then he gives a list: death, life, *angels*, rulers, things present, things to come, powers, height, depth, and anything else in all creation. The list moves from the biggest human experiences to the whole unseen world.

Some words in the list are easy to read. Death and life, present and future, need little explanation. Others are harder. 'Height' and 'depth' were words sometimes used in ancient star-watching for the highest and lowest points of the stars in the sky. Some scholars think Paul had those ideas in mind. Others think he simply meant 'anything above or below'. Either way, Paul's point is that nothing anywhere is strong enough to break God's love.

For Heiser, the list shows how Paul saw the unseen world. Angels, rulers and powers were real to Paul, he argued, and some of them opposed God. Yet Paul places them all under the phrase 'any other created thing'. They are creatures, not rivals equal to God. Readers who do not share Heiser's view still see Romans 8 as a statement of comfort. It is meant to steady people, not to make them afraid.

words.d: in the Bible, heavenly beings, often messengers; Greek angeloi
everything God made, in heaven and on earth, as the Bible describes it
to pull apart or keep apart

look.title: Romans 8:38–39
look.text: For I am persuaded, that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor powers, nor things present, nor things to come, Nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature, shall be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord.
look.prompt: Sort the list into pairs where you can. Which items are about time, which about place, and which about beings? What does 'any other creature' tell you about the powers?

check.q: What does Paul say angels, rulers and powers cannot do in Romans 8:38–39?
choices: Separate believers from the love of God in Christ
check.why: Romans 8:38–39 says none of these can separate believers from God's love in Christ.

check.q: What might 'height' and 'depth' have meant to some ancient readers?
choices: The highest and lowest points of the stars in the sky
check.why: Some scholars note that these words were used in ancient star-watching; others read them as 'above and below'.

check.q: According to Heiser, what does the phrase 'any other creature' show?
choices: The powers do not exist at all
The powers are human kings only
The powers are created beings, not rivals equal to God
check.why: Heiser read the list as placing all the powers under the category of created things.

sections.title: The Gods of the Nations Again

lessons.title: Back to Deuteronomy 32
lessons.mainIdea: Heiser argued that Paul's powers are the sons of God set over the nations in Deuteronomy 32:8, now in rebellion.
reading: Deuteronomy 32:8 says that when the Most High divided the nations, he set their borders by a number. In the traditional Hebrew text, the *Masoretic Text*, the number matches the 'sons of Israel'. But a Hebrew manuscript from the Dead Sea Scrolls reads 'sons of God'. The ancient Greek translation, the *Septuagint*, has 'angels of God'. Many scholars, Heiser included, think 'sons of God' was the earlier reading.

Heiser built much of his work on that reading. In his view, Deuteronomy 32:8–9 says God placed the nations under lesser divine beings after Babel, but kept Israel as his own. Deuteronomy 4:19 and 32:17 add that other nations served these beings. Psalm 82 pictures God judging the gods for ruling unjustly. Daniel 10 names a prince of Persia and a prince of Greece who resist a heavenly messenger.

Heiser argued that Paul read his Bible with this picture in mind. The rulers and authorities of Paul's letters, he said, are these same beings, the gods of the nations. That explains why Paul uses words of territory and rule. It also explains why Paul, sent to the non-Jewish nations, talks so much about the powers. Some scholars accept this link. Others think Paul's words are more general, or that he mainly meant human and social powers.

words.d: the traditional Hebrew text of the Hebrew Bible, copied with great care by Jewish scribes in the Middle Ages
the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible, begun around the 3rd century BCE
a Hebrew Bible phrase for heavenly beings, as in Job 38:7 and, in some manuscripts, Deuteronomy 32:8

look.title: Three Versions of One Verse
look.text: Deuteronomy 32:8 ends in three ways. The Masoretic Text: 'according to the number of the sons of Israel'. A Dead Sea Scrolls manuscript: 'according to the number of the sons of God'. The Septuagint: 'according to the number of the angels of God'.
look.prompt: Which two versions agree most closely? If the verse speaks of heavenly beings, how might that change the way you read Paul's 'rulers and authorities'?

check.q: What does the Dead Sea Scrolls manuscript of Deuteronomy 32:8 read?
check.why: A Dead Sea Scrolls manuscript reads 'sons of God', close to the Septuagint's 'angels of God'.

check.q: What is the Septuagint?
choices: The ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible
check.why: The Septuagint is the ancient Greek translation, begun around the 3rd century BCE.

check.q: Which passage names a prince of Persia and a prince of Greece?
check.why: Daniel 10 tells of a prince of Persia and a prince of Greece resisting a heavenly messenger.

lessons.title: Sacrifices to Daimonia
lessons.mainIdea: In 1 Corinthians 10:20 Paul echoes Deuteronomy 32:17, saying sacrifices to idols are offered to daimonia, not to God.
reading: In Corinth, a Greek city, meat was often sacrificed at temples before it was sold or served. Christians there asked Paul whether they could eat it. In 1 Corinthians 8 and 10, Paul answers carefully. An idol is nothing, he says, just carved wood or stone. But then he adds something in 10:20. What the nations sacrifice, they sacrifice to *daimonia*, not to God, and he does not want believers to share with them.

Paul is echoing Deuteronomy 32:17. That verse says Israel sacrificed to *shedim*, not to God, to gods they had not known. The Septuagint translates shedim with the Greek daimonia. Paul uses the same Greek word. The King James Version translates it 'devils' in both places. Modern translations usually say 'demons'. In Paul's world, daimonia could mean any lesser spiritual beings.

Heiser saw this echo as strong evidence for his view. Paul knew his Deuteronomy 32, Heiser argued, and he read the gods of the nations as real spiritual beings, lesser than God and in rebellion. The idol itself was nothing, but something stood behind it. Other scholars agree Paul is quoting Deuteronomy but read it more simply. They say Paul's main point is loyalty: believers cannot share in two tables at once (10:21).

words.d: Greek for lesser spiritual beings; the King James Version says 'devils', modern translations 'demons'
a Hebrew word in Deuteronomy 32:17 for beings Israel sacrificed to, likely borrowed from an Akkadian word for protective spirits
a carved image used in worship

look.title: 1 Corinthians 10:20
look.text: But I say, that the things which the Gentiles sacrifice, they sacrifice to devils, and not to God: and I would not that ye should have fellowship with devils.
look.cite: 1 Corinthians 10:20, King James Version (1611); compare Deuteronomy 32:17
look.prompt: Compare this with Deuteronomy 32:17, which says Israel sacrificed to devils, not to God. What words match? Why might Paul borrow Moses' words here?

check.q: Which Hebrew Bible verse does Paul echo in 1 Corinthians 10:20?
check.why: Deuteronomy 32:17 says Israel sacrificed to shedim, not to God; Paul repeats the idea with daimonia.

check.q: How does the Septuagint translate the Hebrew shedim in Deuteronomy 32:17?
check.why: The Septuagint uses daimonia, the same Greek word Paul uses in 1 Corinthians 10:20.

check.q: What do other scholars see as Paul's main point in 1 Corinthians 10:20–21?
choices: Idols are more powerful than God
Loyalty: believers cannot share two tables at once
check.why: Many scholars stress loyalty; 10:21 says one cannot share the Lord's table and the table of daimonia.

lessons.title: The Rulers of This Age
lessons.mainIdea: First Corinthians 2:8 says the rulers of this age would not have crucified the Lord of glory had they understood; readers debate who they are.
reading: In 1 Corinthians 2:6–8, Paul speaks of a hidden wisdom of God. He says none of the *rulers of this age* understood it. If they had, he says, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory. The Greek word for rulers here is *archontes*. The same word can mean human officials or spiritual rulers. Paul adds that these rulers are 'passing away' or 'coming to nothing' (2:6).

One reading says the rulers are the humans who took part in the crucifixion: Pilate, Herod and the temple leaders. Acts 4:26–27 uses 'rulers' this way, naming Herod and Pontius Pilate. A second reading says the rulers are spiritual powers. A third reading holds both. It says spiritual powers worked through human officials. Many scholars today take one of the last two views.

Heiser held the spiritual reading strongly. He argued that the powers did not understand God's plan. They thought killing Jesus would be their victory, but the cross was their defeat. Had they known, he said, they would have stopped it. For Heiser, this explains why God's plan was kept hidden in the Hebrew Bible, and why Paul calls it a mystery now made known. Readers who favor the human reading point to how 'rulers' is used in the Gospels and Acts.

words.d: the phrase in 1 Corinthians 2:6–8 for those who did not understand God's hidden wisdom
Greek for rulers; used for both human officials and spiritual powers
in Paul's letters, something once hidden and now made known

look.title: Who Crucified the Lord of Glory?
look.text: Reading 1: the rulers are Pilate, Herod and the temple leaders (compare Acts 4:26–27). Reading 2: the rulers are spiritual powers who misread God's plan. Reading 3: spiritual powers acted through human rulers. The text: 'None of the rulers of this age understood this; if they had, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory' (1 Corinthians 2:8, paraphrased).
look.prompt: Which reading fits 'passing away' in 2:6 best? Which fits Acts 4:26–27 best? Explain one strength of each.

check.q: What Greek word lies behind 'rulers' in 1 Corinthians 2:6–8?
check.why: Paul uses archontes, a word for rulers that can mean human officials or spiritual powers.

check.q: How did Heiser read the rulers of this age?
choices: As spiritual powers who did not understand that the cross would defeat them
check.why: Heiser argued the powers misread God's plan and would not have crucified Jesus had they understood.

check.q: Which passage supports reading 'rulers' as human officials?
choices: Acts 4:26–27, which names Herod and Pontius Pilate
check.why: Acts 4:26–27 applies the word rulers to Herod and Pilate.

lessons.title: Because of the Angels
lessons.mainIdea: In 1 Corinthians 11:10 Paul says a woman should have authority on her head 'because of the angels', a phrase readers explain in several ways.
reading: First Corinthians 11:2–16 is about how men and women should appear when they pray or prophesy in the gathered church. The passage deals with head coverings and hair, and it is debated on many points. Verse 10 adds a short, puzzling reason. A woman ought to have authority, or a sign of authority, on her head 'because of the angels'. Paul does not explain what he means.

Readers have offered several answers. Around 200 CE, Tertullian linked the phrase to the angels of Genesis 6 who were drawn to human women. Heiser argued for a reading in the same direction. In Reversing Hermon (2017), he connected the phrase to the Watchers story and its concern about the boundary between heaven and earth. Other scholars think of angels as present in worship. Some Dead Sea Scrolls describe angels as joining the community's gathering, so good order mattered.

Still other readers focus on the Greek word *exousia*, 'authority'. They read verse 10 as saying the woman herself has authority over her own head. The whole passage is sensitive. It deals with gender roles, and churches today apply it in very different ways. Some keep head coverings in worship, and many do not. A careful reader can lay out each view of 'because of the angels' without deciding the wider questions for anyone else.

words.d: Greek for authority or right; the word in 1 Corinthians 11:10
to speak a message believed to come from God
a veil or cloth worn on the head, discussed in 1 Corinthians 11:2–16

look.title: Four Readings of One Phrase
look.text: 'Because of the angels' (1 Corinthians 11:10). Reading 1 (Tertullian; Heiser): it recalls the Watchers of Genesis 6. Reading 2: angels are present in worship and care about good order. Reading 3: angels are models of honoring God's order. Reading 4: the focus is the woman's own authority, and 'because of the angels' supports it.
look.prompt: Which reading uses the most information from outside Paul's letters? Which stays closest to the passage itself? Why might both approaches be useful?

check.q: What does the Greek word exousia mean?
check.why: Exousia means authority or right; it is the word Paul uses in 1 Corinthians 11:10.

check.q: Which early writer linked 'because of the angels' to the angels of Genesis 6?
check.why: Tertullian, around 200 CE, linked the phrase to the angels drawn to human women in Genesis 6.

check.q: Why do some scholars connect this verse to angels present in worship?
choices: Genesis 5 says angels built the church
Paul says the angels wrote the letter
Some Dead Sea Scrolls describe angels joining the community's gathering
check.why: Some Dead Sea Scrolls picture angels present in the community's gathering, so good order mattered.

lessons.title: Elemental Spirits
lessons.mainIdea: Galatians 4:3, 9 and Colossians 2:8, 20 speak of the stoicheia, a Greek word read as basic principles, physical elements or spiritual beings.
reading: In Galatians 4:3, Paul says that before Christ came, 'we' were enslaved under the *stoicheia* of the world. In 4:9 he calls them weak and poor, and asks the Galatians why they want to be enslaved to them again. Colossians 2:8 and 2:20 use the same word. The King James Version says 'elements' or 'rudiments'. Some modern translations say 'elemental spirits'. The translation depends on the reading.

Stoicheia is a Greek word for things in a row, like the letters of the alphabet. It can mean basic principles, the ABCs of a subject. It can mean the physical elements, which Greeks listed as earth, water, air and fire. By the early centuries CE, some writers also used it for spiritual beings linked to the elements or the stars. So there are three main readings: basic principles, physical elements, or spiritual powers.

Galatians 4:8 is often part of the debate. There Paul says the Galatians once served beings that by nature are not gods. Readers who see the stoicheia as spiritual beings, as the divine-council reading tends to, connect 4:8 with 4:9. They see Paul describing the powers behind the nations' religions. Readers who favor 'basic principles' note that Paul is talking about the law and religious calendars in 4:10. Scholars have not reached one answer.

words.d: Greek for things in a row; read as basic principles, physical elements or spiritual beings
the most basic parts of a subject; the King James wording in Colossians 2:8
in Greek thought, the basic materials earth, water, air and fire

look.title: Galatians 4:8–10
look.text: Paraphrased: Before you knew God, you served beings that are not really gods (4:8). Now that you know God, how can you turn back to the weak and poor stoicheia and want to serve them again (4:9)? You keep special days, months, seasons and years (4:10).
look.prompt: Does verse 8 or verse 10 fit best with each reading of stoicheia? Choose one reading and explain which verse supports it.

check.q: What is the basic meaning of the Greek word stoicheia?
choices: Things in a row, like the letters of the alphabet
check.why: Stoicheia means things in a row, and so came to mean basic parts, elements or ABCs.

check.q: Which verse says the Galatians once served beings that by nature are not gods?
check.why: Galatians 4:8 describes the Galatians' former service to beings that are not gods by nature.

check.q: What is one of the three main readings of stoicheia?
choices: The names of the twelve tribes
Physical elements such as earth, water, air and fire
check.why: Readers take stoicheia as basic principles, physical elements or spiritual beings.

lessons.title: Other Ways to Read the Powers
lessons.mainIdea: Scholars have read Paul's powers as spiritual beings, as structures of human society, or as both, and Heiser's view belongs to this wider debate.
reading: In the twentieth century, scholars argued a great deal about Paul's powers. The Dutch theologian Hendrikus Berkhof, in Christ and the Powers (1953 in Dutch), read them as the structures that hold society together. These include the state, tradition, morality and religion. They can serve people or trap them. The British scholar G. B. Caird's Principalities and Powers (1956) also explored how the powers relate to law and government.

In the 1980s and 1990s, the American scholar Walter Wink wrote a series of books starting with Naming the Powers (1984). Wink read the powers as the inner spirit of institutions, such as a company, a nation or an army. In 1992, Clinton E. Arnold's Powers of Darkness argued the other way. He said Paul's first readers understood the powers as personal spiritual beings, as many Jewish writings of that time did.

Heiser stood with those who read the powers as personal spiritual beings. His special contribution was the link to Deuteronomy 32 and the divine council. For him, the powers are the rebel gods of the nations. Many readers now combine views. They hold that Paul meant spiritual beings, and that those beings work through human systems. Knowing these options helps you see what is at stake in each reading.

words.d: lasting patterns of society, such as governments, laws and traditions
an organization or custom that lasts over time, such as a school, a government or a church
beings with minds and will of their own, not only forces or systems

look.title: A Century of Books on the Powers
look.cite: First publication years of each book (Berkhof's in Dutch)
look.prompt: Which of these writers read the powers mainly as structures, and which as personal beings? What changed between 1953 and 2015?

check.q: How did Hendrikus Berkhof read Paul's powers?
choices: As structures that hold society together, such as the state and tradition
As the Titans of Greek stories
check.why: Berkhof's Christ and the Powers (1953) read the powers as structures of society.

check.q: Who read the powers as the inner spirit of institutions?
check.why: Walter Wink, starting with Naming the Powers (1984), read them as the inner spirit of institutions.

check.q: What was Heiser's special contribution to this debate?
choices: Writing the first book on the powers
Linking the powers to Deuteronomy 32 and the divine council
Proving the powers are only human governments
check.why: Heiser read the powers as personal beings and tied them to the gods of the nations in Deuteronomy 32.

lessons.title: Disarmed at the Cross
lessons.mainIdea: Colossians 2:15 says Christ disarmed the rulers and authorities and led them in a public triumph, using an image from Roman victory parades.
reading: Colossians 2:13–15 describes what the writer says God did through the cross. It speaks of forgiveness and of a record of debt canceled and nailed to the cross. Then verse 15 turns to the powers. God disarmed the rulers and authorities, made a public show of them and triumphed over them in it. The King James Version says 'spoiled', an old word meaning 'stripped'.

The picture comes from Roman life. After a big victory, a Roman general could hold a *triumph*, a parade through Rome. The defeated leaders were led along, stripped of their weapons, for all to see. The Greek verb in Colossians 2:15, thriambeuō, means to lead in such a triumph. The same verb appears in 2 Corinthians 2:14. The image is surprising. A cross was a sign of shame, but here it becomes a victory parade.

Heiser saw Colossians 2:15 as the center of Paul's teaching about the powers. The cross, which looked like the powers' win, was their loss. This fits his reading of 1 Corinthians 2:8. Other readers stress that Colossians places this victory next to forgiveness, so the defeat of the powers and the canceling of debt belong together. Readers of Berkhof's and Wink's kind see the cross as exposing unjust human systems. All agree the verse pictures a public reversal.

words.d: a Roman victory parade in which defeated enemies were led through the city
Greek for 'to lead in a triumph', used in Colossians 2:15 and 2 Corinthians 2:14
to take away someone's weapons or power

look.title: Colossians 2:15
look.text: And having spoiled principalities and powers, he made a shew of them openly, triumphing over them in it.
look.prompt: Find the three actions in this verse. How does knowing about Roman triumphs change the way you picture the scene?

check.q: What was a Roman triumph?
choices: A victory parade with defeated enemies led through the city
check.why: A triumph was a parade after a big victory, with defeated leaders shown to the crowd.

check.q: What does the King James word 'spoiled' mean in Colossians 2:15?
check.why: In older English, 'spoiled' meant stripped, as of weapons or goods.

check.q: How did Heiser connect Colossians 2:15 with 1 Corinthians 2:8?
choices: Both name the prince of Persia
The cross looked like the powers' win but was their loss
check.why: Heiser argued the powers misread the cross, which became their defeat.

lessons.title: Wisdom Shown to the Powers
lessons.mainIdea: Ephesians 3:10 says God's wisdom is made known through the church to the rulers and authorities, which Heiser read as the nations being reclaimed.
reading: Ephesians 3 describes a mystery now revealed. The mystery is that non-Jewish people, the nations, now share fully in God's promise with Israel (3:6). Then 3:10 says something striking. Through the church, God's many-sided wisdom is now made known to the rulers and authorities in the heavenly places. The church itself becomes a message to the powers.

Heiser read this against Deuteronomy 32:8–9. If God had placed the nations under lesser beings after Babel, then Jews and non-Jews joining together would be a sign. The nations were being reclaimed. For Heiser, this was part of what he called the forgotten mission of Jesus Christ, the title theme of Reversing Hermon (2017). The powers would see their territories being won back, not by force, but by people from every nation joining one family.

Other readers stress the human side of Ephesians. For them, the key is peace between Jews and non-Jews, who had been divided (2:14–16). The powers are the audience, but the reconciled community is the point. Readers of many views can agree that Ephesians links the unseen realm with a very visible community. It pictures ordinary people from different nations sharing meals, worship and life.

words.d: in the Bible, the peoples of the world other than Israel; also called Gentiles
to take back something that belonged to you
to bring back together people who were divided

look.title: An Audience in the Heavenly Places
look.text: Ephesians 3:10, paraphrased: through the church, God's many-sided wisdom is now shown to the rulers and authorities in the heavenly places. Ephesians 2:14–16, paraphrased: Christ has made the two groups, Jews and non-Jews, into one and broken down the wall between them.
look.prompt: How does Heiser's reading connect these two passages? How would a reader who focuses on the human side explain them?

check.q: According to Ephesians 3:10, to whom is God's wisdom made known through the church?
choices: The rulers and authorities in the heavenly places
check.why: Ephesians 3:10 says God's wisdom is made known to the rulers and authorities in the heavenly places.

check.q: What mystery does Ephesians 3:6 describe?
choices: The nations share fully in God's promise with Israel
The name of the seventh from Adam
check.why: Ephesians 3:6 says non-Jewish people now share fully in the promise.

review.q: Which Greek word does the King James Version translate as 'principalities'?
review.why: Archai means rulers or beginnings, translated 'principalities' in the King James Version.

review.q: Which verse says the struggle is not against flesh and blood?
review.why: Ephesians 6:12 says the struggle is against rulers and powers in the heavenly places.

review.q: What link did Heiser see between Paul's powers and Deuteronomy 32:8?
choices: The powers are the sons of God set over the nations, now in rebellion
The powers are the Roman army
The powers are the twelve tribes
review.why: Heiser read Paul's powers as the gods of the nations described in Deuteronomy 32:8.

review.q: Paul's word daimonia in 1 Corinthians 10:20 echoes which verse?
review.why: Deuteronomy 32:17 in the Septuagint uses daimonia for the beings Israel sacrificed to.

review.q: Which statement fits Heiser's reading of 1 Corinthians 2:8?
choices: Paul was writing about Greek philosophers
Spiritual rulers would not have crucified Jesus had they understood God's plan
The verse is about the flood
review.why: Heiser argued the rulers of this age were spiritual powers who misread the cross.

review.q: Which reading of 1 Corinthians 11:10 did Tertullian and Heiser share?
choices: 'Because of the angels' recalls the angels of Genesis 6
The verse is about music in worship
review.why: Tertullian and Heiser both connected the phrase to the Genesis 6 story.

choices: A Roman triumph, a victory parade
review.why: The verb thriambeuō pictures leading defeated enemies in a Roman triumph.

review.q: Which scholar read the powers as the inner spirit of institutions?
review.why: Walter Wink, beginning with Naming the Powers (1984), read the powers this way.
